# Factor Graphs, Manifolds, and Modern Back-ends {#sec-advanced-slam}

::: {.callout-note title="Advanced topics chapter: not assessed"}
This chapter goes beyond the course projects. Nothing here is a project
requirement, and no library beyond NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib is needed to run
its examples. It is written for the student who wants to read a modern SLAM or
visual-inertial paper, or open the source of a production estimator, and
recognize every moving part.
:::

Over the last several chapters the book has handed you a box of parts. The
Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoother (@sec-kf-smoothing) revisited the past with future
data. The information filter (@sec-information-filter-marginalization-conditioning)
showed that forgetting a variable is a Schur complement, and that forgetting
makes matrices dense. The error-state filter (@sec-ekf-error-state-filtering)
kept attitude on the rotation group and estimated only a small error. The loop
closure chapter built an $SE(2)$ pose graph from scratch and solved it with
sparse Gauss-Newton (@sec-loop-closure-pose-graph). The visual-navigation chapter
introduced IMU preintegration and the MSCKF (@sec-visual-nav-vio). This chapter
is the exploded-view drawing that shows how those parts fit together in a modern
estimation back end.

Three ideas carry the whole structure. **Factor graphs** say what is being
estimated and what each measurement says about it, and they turn navigation into
sparse nonlinear least squares. **Manifolds** say how to do calculus on
attitudes and poses, which are not vectors no matter how much we would like them
to be. **Marginalization** says how to forget the past without lying about it.
Each gets a section with working code. The chapter then closes with shorter
tours of research directions (resilient navigation, mapping, hybrid filters,
learned components) and some advice on reading the literature.

None of this is new in spirit. Photogrammetrists were adjusting "bundles" of
rays by sparse least squares in the late 1950s [@triggs2000], and the RTS
smoother appeared in an aerospace journal in 1965 [@rauch1965]. What changed
is that sparse solvers, manifold calculus, and cheap computers made it routine
to run these batch ideas onboard, in real time, over thousands of states.

## Factor Graphs and Smoothing {#sec-advanced-slam-factor-graphs-smoothing}

### The Factor-Graph View of Navigation {#sec-advanced-slam-factor-graph-view}

A **factor graph** is a bipartite graph with two kinds of nodes: *variables*
(the unknowns: poses, velocities, IMU biases, landmarks, clock offsets,
calibration parameters) and *factors* (the probabilistic constraints among them:
measurements, motion models, and priors) [@dellaert2017factor]. A factor is
connected to exactly the variables it depends on. Write $\mathcal{X}$ for the
set of all variables, $\mathcal{X}_k \subset \mathcal{X}$ for those touched by
factor $k$, and $\mathcal{Z}$ for the measurements. The posterior factorizes as
a product of factors, and with Gaussian noise each factor is the exponential of
a squared Mahalanobis residual:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\mathcal{X} \mid \mathcal{Z}) &\propto \prod_k \phi_k(\mathcal{X}_k), \\
\phi_k(\mathcal{X}_k) &\propto \exp\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\left\|\mathbf{h}_k(\mathcal{X}_k) \ominus \mathbf{z}_k\right\|^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k}\right), \\
\mathcal{X}^\star &= \arg\min_{\mathcal{X}} \sum_k \left\|\mathbf{h}_k(\mathcal{X}_k) \ominus \mathbf{z}_k\right\|^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-advanced-slam-map}

with $\|\mathbf{e}\|^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = \mathbf{e}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{e}$.
The maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate is a nonlinear least-squares problem,
which is the GraphSLAM statement of @sec-slam-graphslam-one-page and the pose
graph cost of @eq-loop-closure-pose-graph-cost with more kinds of factors. The
$\ominus$ is there because some measurements live on manifolds; it is the
subject of @sec-advanced-slam-lie-groups. A prior is just a factor attached to a
single variable, so "prior" and "measurement" stop being different concepts.

The graph view is valuable because it is indifferent to where a measurement came
from. @tbl-advanced-slam-factors lists the factors in a typical
visual-inertial-GNSS navigation system, and @fig-advanced-slam-factor-graph draws
a small instance.

| Factor | Variables touched | Residual |
|---|---|---|
| Prior (initial or marginal) | one state, or a set of states | state $\ominus$ prior mean |
| IMU preintegration | states $i$, $j$ and biases | rotation, velocity, position increments |
| Bias random walk | biases at $i$, $j$ | $\mathbf{b}_j - \mathbf{b}_i$ |
| Camera reprojection | one pose and one landmark | pixel minus projection |
| Lidar or radar scan match | two poses | relative pose $\ominus$ measured |
| Wheel or DVL odometry | two poses (or one velocity) | relative motion $\ominus$ measured |
| GNSS position, pseudorange, Doppler | one state (and clock) | measured minus predicted |
| Barometer, depth, magnetometer | one state | measured minus predicted |
| Loop closure | two distant poses | relative pose $\ominus$ measured |

Solving @eq-advanced-slam-map works exactly as in the loop-closure chapter.
Linearize every residual at the current estimate,
$\mathbf{e}_k(\mathcal{X} \oplus \boldsymbol{\delta}) \approx \mathbf{e}_k + \mathbf{J}_k\boldsymbol{\delta}$,
whiten each one by $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1/2}$, and stack them into a tall
sparse system $\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\delta} \approx -\mathbf{r}$. Its normal
equations are $\mathbf{H}\boldsymbol{\delta} = -\mathbf{b}$ with
$\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ (@eq-loop-closure-normal-equations), and
block $(i, j)$ of $\mathbf{H}$ is nonzero only if some factor touches both
variable $i$ and variable $j$. The sparsity pattern of $\mathbf{H}$ *is* the
graph, with each factor folded into edges among its variables. Square-root SAM
[@dellaert2006] factors $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}$ instead, or
equivalently $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{R}^T\mathbf{R}$ by Cholesky, and solves the
triangular system $\mathbf{R}\boldsymbol{\delta} = -\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{r}$.

### Filtering, Fixed-Lag Smoothing, and Full Smoothing {#sec-advanced-slam-filter-smoother-spectrum}

Given a factor graph, the main design decision is which variables to keep.
@tbl-advanced-slam-spectrum lays out the three standard answers.

| Estimator | Variables kept | What happens to old states | What gets relinearized |
|---|---|---|---|
| Filter (EKF, ESKF, MSCKF) | the current state (plus landmarks in EKF-SLAM, clones in the MSCKF) | marginalized immediately | only the current state, once per update |
| Fixed-lag smoother | the states in a sliding window | marginalized into a prior factor when they leave the window | everything in the window, every iteration |
| Full smoother (batch or incremental) | every state | kept | everything (incrementally: whatever has moved) |

: The filter-smoother spectrum. {#tbl-advanced-slam-spectrum}

The three are closer relatives than they look. Take the linear-Gaussian chain of
@sec-kf, with one factor per dynamics step and one per measurement, and solve it
by sparse Gaussian elimination in time order. Eliminating $\mathbf{x}_0$
combines its prior, its measurement, and the dynamics factor into a Gaussian
factor on $\mathbf{x}_1$: a Kalman update at time 0 followed by a prediction to
time 1. Keep going and the last elimination leaves the filter's posterior on
$\mathbf{x}_N$. Back-substitution then sweeps backward through the conditionals
that elimination produced and returns the RTS smoothed means of @eq-kf-rts (the
smoothed covariances follow from the same conditionals). *The Kalman
filter is the forward sweep of sparse elimination on a chain, and the RTS
smoother is the back-substitution* [@dellaert2017factor]. For a linear-Gaussian
problem all three estimators in @tbl-advanced-slam-spectrum give the same
estimate of the newest state; they differ only in what they can say about the
past.

For nonlinear problems they really do differ, and the difference is
relinearization. A filter linearizes each measurement once, at whatever the
estimate happened to be when the measurement arrived, and that choice is baked
in forever (@sec-loop-closure-why-filtering-slam). A smoother keeps the
variables and relinearizes them as the estimate improves. A fixed-lag smoother is
the compromise most real-time visual-inertial and lidar-inertial systems choose:
relinearize the recent past, where the estimate is still moving, and marginalize
the distant past into a prior factor (@sec-advanced-slam-marginalization). Full
smoothing is what you run when you need the whole trajectory right, such as for
mapping, survey post-processing, or a flight-test reference trajectory. Keeping
a window of states also makes late measurements easy. An acoustic fix that
arrives two seconds after it was taken, or a GNSS solution delayed by
processing, is simply a factor attached to the state at its own timestamp; as
long as that state is still in the window, nothing has to be rolled back and
reprocessed, which is the hard part of handling delayed measurements in a
filter (@sec-practical-time-sync).

One consequence matters for the rest of the stack. A smoother revises the past,
and when a loop closure arrives it may revise the *present* by meters. A
controller fed that estimate would see a step, which is exactly what control
loops must not see. Production systems therefore publish two things: a smooth,
continuous, locally accurate odometry estimate for control, and a separate,
slowly updated correction that carries it into the global frame for planning.
ROS encodes the pattern as its `map`, `odom`, and `base_link` frames (in ROS's
ENU world and FLU body axes [@rep103]; from the book's NED and FRD, swap north
and east and negate down for the world frame, negate $y$ and $z$ for the body
frame, and reorder quaternions to ROS's scalar-last convention). @sec-practical
develops the interface; the point here is that the choice of back end shapes
what navigation can promise downstream.

### Sparsity and Variable Ordering {#sec-advanced-slam-ordering}

Elimination has a cost that depends on the order. Eliminating a variable means
collecting every factor that touches it, forming the joint Gaussian of the
variable and its neighbors (its *separator*), and splitting that into a
conditional for the variable and a new factor on the separator. The conditional
becomes one block row of $\mathbf{R}$. The new factor is exactly the Schur
complement of @eq-information-marginal, so it connects *every pair* of the
eliminated variable's neighbors. Eliminating a variable is marginalizing it, and
the new connections are **fill-in**, the same fill-in that @fig-information-fill-in
showed for filtering.

Which order minimizes fill-in is NP-hard in general, but greedy heuristics work
very well. The simplest, **minimum degree**, always eliminates the variable with
the fewest current neighbors. Production solvers use refinements such as COLAMD
and METIS. The cell below plays the "elimination game" symbolically on a small
SLAM graph (40 poses in a chain, 16 landmarks each seen by five consecutive
poses, and a revisit at the end that re-observes the first two landmarks) and
counts the nonzeros of $\mathbf{R}$ under three orders. It then checks the
symbolic count against a real Cholesky factorization of a random information
matrix with the same sparsity pattern.

::: {#advanced-slam-ordering .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import scipy.sparse as sp
import scipy.sparse.linalg as spla

# A small SLAM factor graph: a pose chain, landmarks seen by short runs of poses,
# and a revisit at the end where the last three poses see l0 and l1 again.
n_poses, n_landmarks = 40, 16
poses = [f"x{k}" for k in range(n_poses)]
landmarks = [f"l{m}" for m in range(n_landmarks)]
variables = poses + landmarks
factors = [("x0",)]                                             # prior on the first pose
factors += [(poses[k], poses[k + 1]) for k in range(n_poses - 1)]  # odometry
for m in range(n_landmarks):
    first = round(m * (n_poses - 6) / (n_landmarks - 1))
    factors += [(poses[k], landmarks[m]) for k in range(first, first + 5)]
for k in range(n_poses - 3, n_poses):                           # the revisit
    factors += [(poses[k], "l0"), (poses[k], "l1")]


def neighbors(factors):
    """Variable adjacency: two variables are neighbors if a factor touches both."""
    nbrs = {v: set() for v in variables}
    for factor in factors:
        for a in factor:
            nbrs[a].update(b for b in factor if b != a)
    return nbrs


def eliminate(order, factors):
    """Symbolic elimination in the given order.

    Eliminating a variable connects all of its remaining neighbors (the Schur
    complement). Returns the sparsity pattern of the upper-triangular factor R
    (rows and columns in elimination order) and the number of fill-in pairs.
    """
    nbrs = neighbors(factors)
    position = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(order)}
    R = np.eye(len(order), dtype=bool)
    fill = 0
    for v in order:
        separator = nbrs.pop(v)
        for a in separator:
            R[position[v], position[a]] = True
            nbrs[a].discard(v)
        for a in separator:
            new = separator - nbrs[a] - {a}
            nbrs[a] |= new
            fill += len(new)
    return R, fill // 2                     # each new pair was counted from both ends


def minimum_degree_order(factors):
    """Greedy minimum degree: repeatedly eliminate the variable with fewest neighbors."""
    nbrs = neighbors(factors)
    order = []
    while nbrs:
        v = min(nbrs, key=lambda u: (len(nbrs[u]), variables.index(u)))
        separator = nbrs.pop(v)
        for a in separator:
            nbrs[a].discard(v)
            nbrs[a] |= separator - {a}
        order.append(v)
    return order


orders = {
    "poses first (filtering order)": poses + landmarks,
    "landmarks first (BA order)": landmarks + poses,
    "greedy minimum degree": minimum_degree_order(factors),
}

# A random information matrix with this sparsity, for a numerical cross-check.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
index = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(variables)}
H_random = np.zeros((len(variables), len(variables)))
for factor in factors:
    for _ in range(2):                      # two random residual rows per factor
        J = np.zeros(len(variables))
        J[[index[a] for a in factor]] = rng.normal(size=len(factor))
        H_random += np.outer(J, J)

patterns = {}
for name, order in orders.items():
    R, fill = eliminate(order, factors)
    perm = [index[v] for v in order]
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(H_random[np.ix_(perm, perm)])
    patterns[name] = R
    print(f"{name:30s} nonzeros in R: {R.sum():3d} (Cholesky: {(L != 0).sum():3d}),"
          f" fill-in pairs: {fill:3d}")
```

The symbolic counts match the numerical Cholesky factor exactly, which is the
point of the elimination game: fill-in is decided by the graph, before a single
number is computed. The filtering order is the worst of the three, and
@fig-advanced-slam-ordering shows why: once the poses are gone, every landmark
is connected to every other, the dense map of EKF-SLAM in square-root
information form. The bundle-adjustment order, landmarks first, is the reduced camera system
of @eq-visual-nav-schur, and here it leaves fill mostly among nearby poses.
Minimum degree, which knows nothing about poses or landmarks, beats both. For
real problems the differences are not 2:1 but orders of magnitude, which is why
every serious solver computes an ordering before it factors anything.

### Incremental Smoothing and the Bayes Tree {#sec-advanced-slam-bayes-tree}

Elimination does more than solve the linear system. Each eliminated variable
leaves behind a conditional density $p(\theta \mid \text{separator})$, and the
collection of conditionals is a Bayes network that represents the same
posterior. Grouping the conditionals into cliques gives a tree, the **Bayes
tree**, whose root holds the last variables eliminated, normally the most recent
states [@kaess2012isam2].

The tree explains what changes when a new measurement arrives. A factor that
touches only recent variables affects only the cliques that contain them and
their ancestors on the path to the root. Everything else in the tree, which is
almost all of the past, is untouched and is reused as is. iSAM2 exploits this:
it detaches the affected top of the tree, turns it back into factors, adds the
new factors, re-eliminates just that piece with a fresh local ordering (a
constrained COLAMD that keeps the newest variables near the root), and reattaches
it [@kaess2012isam2]. It also relinearizes only variables whose estimates have
drifted more than a threshold from their linearization points, so a smooth
trajectory is relinearized rarely and a loop closure triggers relinearization
along the loop. The incremental-smoothing paragraph of the loop-closure chapter
(@sec-loop-closure-incremental-smoothing) gives the cost intuition: an odometry
update is nearly free, a loop closure costs roughly the length of the loop.
iSAM2 is the incremental descendant of square-root SAM [@dellaert2006], which
first showed that keeping the whole trajectory and factoring the sparse
square-root information matrix beats carrying a dense filter covariance.

### Software {#sec-advanced-slam-software}

You do not need any of these libraries for this course, but you will meet them
the moment you open a modern navigation code base. **GTSAM**, from Dellaert's
group at Georgia Tech, implements factor graphs, iSAM2, on-manifold pose and
rotation types, and the preintegrated IMU factor; it has Python bindings, and
LIO-SAM is built on it. **g2o** is a general graph optimizer used by ORB-SLAM.
**Ceres Solver**, from Google, is a general robustified nonlinear least-squares
library with automatic differentiation and manifold support, and it is the
optimizer inside VINS-Mono and OKVIS. All three speak the language of this
chapter: variables that live on manifolds with a $\oplus$, factors with
residuals, noise models and robust kernels, and a sparse solver with an
ordering. If you can write the factor and its Jacobian, the library does the
rest.

## Visual-Inertial Odometry as a Factor Graph {#sec-advanced-slam-visual-inertial-odometry}

The visual-navigation chapter covers VIO in detail: the MSCKF and its null-space
trick (@sec-visual-nav-msckf), IMU preintegration
(@sec-visual-nav-preintegration), the four unobservable directions
(@sec-visual-nav-vio-observability), and the systems worth knowing by name
(@sec-visual-nav-vi-systems). The combination works because the two sensors fail
in complementary ways (@tbl-advanced-slam-vio-sensors):

| Sensor | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| Camera | Rich geometric constraints from the environment | Sensitive to lighting, blur, texture, and scale ambiguity |
| IMU | High-rate short-term motion, metric scale, and the gravity direction | Bias-driven drift when used alone |

: Why cameras and IMUs are fused. {#tbl-advanced-slam-vio-sensors}

In factor-graph terms, optimization-based VIO is the graph of
@fig-advanced-slam-factor-graph without the GNSS factor. Each keyframe $i$ has a
state with attitude $\mathbf{C}_i = \mathbf{C}_{b_i}^n$, velocity
$\mathbf{v}_i$, position $\mathbf{p}_i$, and IMU biases. The preintegrated
increments $\Delta\mathbf{C}_{ij}$, $\Delta\mathbf{v}_{ij}$, and
$\Delta\mathbf{p}_{ij}$ of @eq-visual-nav-preintegration become one factor
between keyframes $i$ and $j$, whose residuals compare the increments with the
keyframe states [@forster2017preintegration]:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{r}_{\Delta C} &= \operatorname{Log}\left(\Delta\mathbf{C}_{ij}^T\,\mathbf{C}_i^T\mathbf{C}_j\right), \\
\mathbf{r}_{\Delta v} &= \mathbf{C}_i^T\left(\mathbf{v}_j - \mathbf{v}_i - \mathbf{g}^n\Delta t_{ij}\right) - \Delta\mathbf{v}_{ij}, \\
\mathbf{r}_{\Delta p} &= \mathbf{C}_i^T\left(\mathbf{p}_j - \mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{v}_i\Delta t_{ij} - \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{g}^n\Delta t_{ij}^2\right) - \Delta\mathbf{p}_{ij}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-advanced-slam-imu-factor}

Each residual vanishes when the keyframe states agree with what the IMU says
happened between them. The increments are corrected to first order for the
current bias estimates, a bias random-walk factor links consecutive biases, and
the rotation residual is a $\operatorname{Log}$ on $SO(3)$, so its Jacobians
need the manifold calculus of the next section. Camera factors attach
reprojection residuals between keyframes and landmarks, and a marginal prior
factor summarizes everything that has slid out of the window.

The well-known systems are different answers to the questions of
@tbl-advanced-slam-spectrum. The MSCKF [@mourikis2007msckf] and OpenVINS
[@geneva2020openvins] are filters over a window of cloned poses, and their
null-space projection is a way of marginalizing each feature the moment its
track ends. OKVIS [@leutenegger2015okvis] and VINS-Mono [@qin2018vins] are
fixed-lag smoothers: they optimize a window of keyframes with preintegrated IMU
factors and reprojection residuals and marginalize the oldest keyframe into a
prior. ORB-SLAM3 [@campos2021orbslam3] adds a persistent map, local bundle
adjustment, and loop closure on top. Lupton and Sukkarieh's original
preintegration paper [@lupton2012visual] was motivated by the same smoothing
view: integrate the IMU once, so that relinearizing a keyframe does not mean
reintegrating hundreds of samples.

## On-Manifold Estimation {#sec-advanced-slam-lie-groups}

Attitude is not a vector. The book has said so since @sec-frames-rotation-vector
and has dealt with it locally: wrap headings (@sec-ukf-angles), keep the
quaternion in the nominal state and estimate a three-component error
(@sec-frames-small-angle-error), use a reset Jacobian after injecting a
correction (@sec-ekf-error-state-filtering). This section collects those tricks
into one systematic method that works for any estimator, filter or smoother,
and for any pose-like variable. The standard references are Barfoot
[@barfoot2017] and Solà's error-state notes and his short "micro Lie theory"
[@sola2017; @sola2018micro], whose notation we mostly follow.

### Groups, Tangent Spaces, Exp, and Log {#sec-advanced-slam-exp-log}

The rotations form the **special orthogonal group**
$SO(3) = \{\mathbf{C} \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3} : \mathbf{C}^T\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{I},\ \det\mathbf{C} = 1\}$.
It is a group (rotations compose and invert) and a smooth three-dimensional
surface inside the nine-dimensional space of matrices: a **Lie group**. Poses
form the **special Euclidean group** $SE(3)$ of homogeneous transforms
$\mathbf{T} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{C} & \mathbf{r} \\ \mathbf{0}^T & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
(@sec-frames-camera-transforms), and planar poses form $SE(2)$, the group of
the loop-closure chapter.

At the identity, a Lie group has a flat **tangent space** of the same dimension:
three numbers for $SO(3)$, six for $SE(3)$, three for $SE(2)$. For $SO(3)$ the
tangent vectors are rotation vectors $\boldsymbol{\phi}$, written as skew
matrices $[\boldsymbol{\phi}]_\times$ when we need them as matrices. Two maps
connect the tangent space with the group:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Exp}(\boldsymbol{\phi}) &= \exp\left([\boldsymbol{\phi}]_\times\right) \in SO(3), \\
\operatorname{Log}\left(\operatorname{Exp}(\boldsymbol{\phi})\right) &= \boldsymbol{\phi},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-advanced-slam-exp-log}

where the second line holds for rotation angles $\|\boldsymbol{\phi}\| < \pi$,
because $\operatorname{Log}$ always returns an angle in $[0, \pi]$.
$\operatorname{Exp}$ is Rodrigues' formula (@eq-frames-rodrigues).
$\operatorname{Log}$ recovers the angle from the trace and the axis from the
skew-symmetric part, with care near $0$ (divide by $\sin\phi$) and near $\pi$
(the skew part vanishes). For $SE(3)$, with tangent vector
$\boldsymbol{\xi} = [\boldsymbol{\rho};\ \boldsymbol{\phi}]$,

$$
\operatorname{Exp}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) =
\begin{bmatrix}
\operatorname{Exp}(\boldsymbol{\phi}) & \mathbf{J}_l(\boldsymbol{\phi})\,\boldsymbol{\rho} \\
\mathbf{0}^T & 1
\end{bmatrix},
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_l$ is the left Jacobian defined below [@barfoot2017]. The
matrix $\mathbf{V}(\phi)$ in the loop-closure chapter's $SE(2)$ logarithm is the
planar version of the same object.

### Plus and Minus, Left and Right {#sec-advanced-slam-plus-minus}

Estimation needs two operations: move an estimate by a small correction
($\oplus$), and measure the difference between two group elements as a vector
($\ominus$). On a group there are two natural choices, depending on which side
the correction multiplies [@sola2018micro]:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{X} \oplus_r \boldsymbol{\tau} &= \mathbf{X}\operatorname{Exp}(\boldsymbol{\tau}), \\
\mathbf{Y} \ominus_r \mathbf{X} &= \operatorname{Log}\left(\mathbf{X}^{-1}\mathbf{Y}\right), \\
\mathbf{X} \oplus_l \boldsymbol{\tau} &= \operatorname{Exp}(\boldsymbol{\tau})\mathbf{X}, \\
\mathbf{Y} \ominus_l \mathbf{X} &= \operatorname{Log}\left(\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{X}^{-1}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-advanced-slam-plus-minus}

For attitude $\mathbf{C}_b^n$ the two sides have physical meanings. A right
perturbation $\mathbf{C}_b^n\operatorname{Exp}(\boldsymbol{\tau})$ rotates the
body frame about axes fixed in the *body*; a left perturbation
$\operatorname{Exp}(\boldsymbol{\tau})\mathbf{C}_b^n$ rotates it about axes fixed
in the *navigation* frame. The book's attitude error convention
(@sec-frames-conventions), $\mathbf{C}_b^n = \operatorname{Exp}(\delta\boldsymbol{\theta})\hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n$,
is the left choice, and "true minus estimate" becomes

$$
\delta\boldsymbol{\theta} = \mathbf{C}_b^n \ominus_l \hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n
= \operatorname{Log}\left(\mathbf{C}_b^n(\hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n)^T\right),
$$

a rotation vector resolved in NED. Its north and east components are tilt
errors and its down component is the heading error, which is why inertial
navigators like this convention. Solà's error-state notes use the right choice,
with $\delta\boldsymbol{\theta}$ resolved in the body frame [@sola2017]. Neither
is more correct. The two are related by the **adjoint**,
$\mathbf{X}\operatorname{Exp}(\boldsymbol{\tau})\mathbf{X}^{-1} = \operatorname{Exp}(\operatorname{Ad}_\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\tau})$,
which for $SO(3)$ is the rotation itself, $\operatorname{Ad}_\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{C}$.
The same attitude can therefore be written both ways,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Exp}(\delta\boldsymbol{\theta}^n)\,\hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n
&= \hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n\operatorname{Exp}(\delta\boldsymbol{\theta}^b), \\
\delta\boldsymbol{\theta}^n &= \hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n\,\delta\boldsymbol{\theta}^b .
\end{aligned}
$$

That is just "resolve a body-frame vector in the navigation frame." For $SE(3)$
with $\boldsymbol{\tau} = [\boldsymbol{\rho};\ \boldsymbol{\phi}]$ the adjoint is
$\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{C} & [\mathbf{r}]_\times\mathbf{C} \\ \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{C} \end{bmatrix}$.
What matters is consistency: the residuals, the Jacobians, the covariance, the
injection, and the reset must all use the same side. Mixing them is the
classic way to get a Jacobian that is wrong by exactly a rotation, and therefore
works perfectly while the vehicle points north (@sec-math-reference-quaternion-kinematics-derivatives).

A pose can live on $SE(3)$ or on the product $SO(3) \times \mathbb{R}^3$. They
differ only in how a correction moves the position: on $SE(3)$ a translation
correction is applied in the rotated frame and couples to the rotation, while on
$SO(3) \times \mathbb{R}^3$ position is corrected additively in NED, as the
error-state filter does. GTSAM's `Pose3` is $SE(3)$; many VIO systems, and the
example below, use the product.

### Jacobians on the Manifold {#sec-advanced-slam-manifold-jacobians}

The derivative of a function of a group element is defined through the
perturbation: perturb the input by a small tangent vector, measure the change of
the output (with $\ominus$ if the output is also on a group), and take the
linear part. The building blocks for $SO(3)$ are the **right and left
Jacobians**,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Exp}(\boldsymbol{\phi} + \delta\boldsymbol{\phi})
&\approx \operatorname{Exp}(\boldsymbol{\phi})\operatorname{Exp}\left(\mathbf{J}_r(\boldsymbol{\phi})\,\delta\boldsymbol{\phi}\right) \\
&\approx \operatorname{Exp}\left(\mathbf{J}_l(\boldsymbol{\phi})\,\delta\boldsymbol{\phi}\right)\operatorname{Exp}(\boldsymbol{\phi}), \\
\operatorname{Log}\left(\mathbf{C}\operatorname{Exp}(\delta\boldsymbol{\phi})\right)
&\approx \operatorname{Log}(\mathbf{C}) + \mathbf{J}_r^{-1}\left(\operatorname{Log}\mathbf{C}\right)\delta\boldsymbol{\phi},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-advanced-slam-jacobian-defs}

which say how a change in the rotation vector maps to a rotation on the right or
on the left, and how $\operatorname{Log}$ responds to a perturbation. In closed
form, with $\phi = \|\boldsymbol{\phi}\|$ [@barfoot2017; @sola2018micro],

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{J}_r(\boldsymbol{\phi}) &= \mathbf{I} - \frac{1 - \cos\phi}{\phi^2}[\boldsymbol{\phi}]_\times
+ \frac{\phi - \sin\phi}{\phi^3}[\boldsymbol{\phi}]_\times^2, \\
\mathbf{J}_l(\boldsymbol{\phi}) &= \mathbf{J}_r(-\boldsymbol{\phi}) = \mathbf{J}_r(\boldsymbol{\phi})^T
= \operatorname{Exp}(\boldsymbol{\phi})\,\mathbf{J}_r(\boldsymbol{\phi}), \\
\mathbf{J}_r^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\phi}) &= \mathbf{I} + \tfrac{1}{2}[\boldsymbol{\phi}]_\times
+ \left(\frac{1}{\phi^2} - \frac{1 + \cos\phi}{2\phi\sin\phi}\right)[\boldsymbol{\phi}]_\times^2 .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-advanced-slam-so3-jacobians}

All three approach $\mathbf{I}$ for small $\phi$, which is why small-angle work
can often ignore them, and none can be ignored when the angle is not small. With
these and the adjoint, the Jacobians of the common operations follow in a line
each (@tbl-advanced-slam-jacobians). Each entry is the matrix that multiplies
the input perturbation to give the output perturbation, for the side named in
the column.

| Operation | Right (body) perturbation | Left (nav) perturbation, the book's |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}$, with respect to $\mathbf{X}$ | $\mathbf{C}_Y^T$ | $\mathbf{I}$ |
| $\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}$, with respect to $\mathbf{Y}$ | $\mathbf{I}$ | $\mathbf{C}_X$ |
| $\mathbf{X}^{-1}$ | $-\mathbf{C}_X$ | $-\mathbf{C}_X^T$ |
| $\mathbf{C}\mathbf{v}$ (output a vector) | $-\mathbf{C}[\mathbf{v}]_\times$ | $-[\mathbf{C}\mathbf{v}]_\times$ |
| $\operatorname{Log}(\mathbf{C})$ (output a vector) | $\mathbf{J}_r^{-1}(\operatorname{Log}\mathbf{C})$ | $\mathbf{J}_l^{-1}(\operatorname{Log}\mathbf{C})$ |

: Jacobians of common $SO(3)$ operations. {#tbl-advanced-slam-jacobians}

The rotation-times-vector rows are @eq-math-reference-jacobian-nav and its
body-frame twin. As an example of the chain rule, take a relative-pose
measurement $(\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{C}}_{ij}, \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{p}}_{ij})$ of
pose $j$ in the body frame of pose $i$, with poses on $SO(3) \times \mathbb{R}^3$:

$$
\mathbf{e}_{ij} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{e}_p \\ \mathbf{e}_\theta
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{C}_i^T(\mathbf{p}_j - \mathbf{p}_i) - \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{p}}_{ij} \\
\operatorname{Log}\left(\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{C}}_{ij}^T\,\mathbf{C}_i^T\mathbf{C}_j\right)
\end{bmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-advanced-slam-relpose-factor}

This is the 3D version of @eq-loop-closure-se2-residual and the same pattern as
the rotation residual of @eq-advanced-slam-imu-factor. Perturb with the book's
convention, $\mathbf{C}_j \leftarrow \operatorname{Exp}(\delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_j)\mathbf{C}_j$
and $\mathbf{p}_j \leftarrow \mathbf{p}_j + \delta\mathbf{p}_j$. Moving the
perturbation through $\mathbf{C}_j$ with the adjoint gives
$\mathbf{C}_i^T\operatorname{Exp}(\delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_j)\mathbf{C}_j = \mathbf{C}_i^T\mathbf{C}_j\operatorname{Exp}(\mathbf{C}_j^T\delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_j)$,
and the $\operatorname{Log}$ rule of @eq-advanced-slam-jacobian-defs finishes
the job. With the state perturbation ordered $\delta\mathbf{x}_i = [\delta\mathbf{p}_i;\ \delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_i]$,
position first as in the error-state filter,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial\mathbf{e}_{ij}}{\partial\delta\mathbf{x}_i} &=
\begin{bmatrix}
-\mathbf{C}_i^T & \mathbf{C}_i^T[\mathbf{p}_j - \mathbf{p}_i]_\times \\
\mathbf{0} & -\mathbf{J}_r^{-1}(\mathbf{e}_\theta)\,\mathbf{C}_j^T
\end{bmatrix}, \\
\frac{\partial\mathbf{e}_{ij}}{\partial\delta\mathbf{x}_j} &=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{C}_i^T & \mathbf{0} \\
\mathbf{0} & \mathbf{J}_r^{-1}(\mathbf{e}_\theta)\,\mathbf{C}_j^T
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-advanced-slam-relpose-jacobians}

Notice that the residual is a body-frame (right) construct while the
perturbation is a navigation-frame (left) one. That is fine, because each
Jacobian is derived for the perturbation the update will actually apply; the
$\mathbf{C}_j^T$ factors are the adjoints that convert between the two sides.

### Covariance on the Manifold {#sec-advanced-slam-manifold-covariance}

A Gaussian on a group is defined in the tangent space at the mean:
$\mathbf{C}_b^n = \operatorname{Exp}(\delta\boldsymbol{\theta})\hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n$
with $\delta\boldsymbol{\theta} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{P})$. The
attitude block of every error-state filter in this book is exactly such a
covariance, resolved in NED. The right-perturbation version of the same
uncertainty has covariance $\hat{\mathbf{C}}^T\mathbf{P}\hat{\mathbf{C}}$, by the
adjoint. Propagation follows from @tbl-advanced-slam-jacobians. For a
composition $\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}$ of independent uncertain
rotations, the left perturbations add as
$\delta\mathbf{z} \approx \delta\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{C}_X\delta\mathbf{y}$, so

$$
\mathbf{P}_Z \approx \mathbf{P}_X + \mathbf{C}_X\,\mathbf{P}_Y\,\mathbf{C}_X^T .
$$

With $\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{C}_{b_k}^n$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ a noisy gyro increment
in the body frame, this is the attitude part of strapdown covariance
propagation: gyro noise is rotated into NED by the current attitude and added.

A Gaussian in tangent coordinates is not a Gaussian in Cartesian coordinates. A
vehicle with a well-known position but an uncertain heading, driven forward
some distance, has a position cloud shaped like a banana, curved along the arc
of possible headings. An ellipse in north and east cannot represent that, while
a Gaussian in the exponential coordinates of the pose represents it well
[@barfoot2017]. This is one more reason to keep uncertainty on the manifold.

### Gauss-Newton on a Manifold {#sec-advanced-slam-manifold-gauss-newton}

Least squares on a manifold changes three things relative to the vector case:
the residual uses $\ominus$, the Jacobians are taken with respect to the tangent
perturbation, and the update is applied with $\oplus$
(@eq-advanced-slam-plus-minus):

1. Linearize: $\mathbf{e}_k(\mathcal{X} \oplus \boldsymbol{\delta}) \approx \mathbf{e}_k(\mathcal{X}) + \mathbf{J}_k\boldsymbol{\delta}$.
2. Solve $\mathbf{H}\boldsymbol{\delta} = -\mathbf{b}$, with $\mathbf{H} = \sum_k \mathbf{J}_k^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}\mathbf{J}_k$ and $\mathbf{b} = \sum_k \mathbf{J}_k^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}\mathbf{e}_k$.
3. Update every variable on its manifold, $\mathcal{X} \leftarrow \mathcal{X} \oplus \boldsymbol{\delta}$, and repeat.

At convergence, $\mathbf{H}^{-1}$ is the covariance of the tangent-space error at
the solution, in the same convention as the $\oplus$. The loop-closure chapter's
additive update of $(x, y, \theta)$ followed by wrapping is a valid $\oplus$ in
2D. In 3D, additive updates to Euler angles or quaternion components are not,
which is why every 3D solver carries an explicit $\oplus$.

The **error-state Kalman filter is the filtering cousin of this idea**. Its
nominal state lives on the manifold; its error state lives in the tangent space
at the nominal (left, in this book); its covariance is a covariance on the
manifold; its measurement update is one linearized Gauss-Newton step in that
tangent space (the iterated EKF of @sec-ekf-iterated-ekf takes several);
injection is the $\oplus$; and the reset moves the tangent space to the new
nominal. The reset Jacobian of @eq-ekf-reset-jacobian is in fact the left
Jacobian, $\mathbf{G} = \mathbf{J}_l(\delta\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})$, truncated
to first order; for Solà's body-frame error it is $\mathbf{J}_r(\delta\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})$,
which explains the sign flip noted in @sec-ekf-error-state-filtering. A filter
takes one tangent-space step per measurement for the current state and never
returns; a smoother takes as many as it likes, for every state, as the estimate
improves.

### $SO(3)$ in Code {#sec-advanced-slam-so3-code}

The cell below implements $\operatorname{Exp}$ and $\operatorname{Log}$
(@eq-advanced-slam-exp-log) and the Jacobians of @eq-advanced-slam-so3-jacobians and checks them numerically:
against SciPy, against finite differences of their definitions, against each
other, and against the error-state reset. Two implementation details deserve a
comment. $\operatorname{Log}$ computes the angle with `arctan2` of the sine and
cosine rather than `arccos` of the cosine, because `arccos` near $\pm 1$ turns
a rounding error of $10^{-16}$ into an angle error of $10^{-8}$; and near
$\pi$, where the skew-symmetric part carries no axis information, it reads the
axis from the symmetric part.

::: {#advanced-slam-so3 .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from scipy.spatial.transform import Rotation


def skew(a):
    """[a]_x, so that skew(a) @ b == np.cross(a, b)."""
    return np.array([[0.0, -a[2], a[1]], [a[2], 0.0, -a[0]], [-a[1], a[0], 0.0]])


def vee(A):
    """Inverse of skew: the vector a with [a]_x = A."""
    return np.array([A[2, 1], A[0, 2], A[1, 0]])


def so3_exp(phi):
    """Exp: rotation vector -> rotation matrix (Rodrigues' formula)."""
    angle = np.linalg.norm(phi)
    K = skew(phi)
    if angle < 1e-8:
        return np.eye(3) + K + 0.5 * K @ K               # Taylor series near zero
    return (np.eye(3) + np.sin(angle) / angle * K
            + (1.0 - np.cos(angle)) / angle**2 * K @ K)


def so3_log(C):
    """Log: rotation matrix -> rotation vector with angle in [0, pi]."""
    w = 0.5 * vee(C - C.T)                               # = sin(angle) * axis
    cos_angle = 0.5 * (np.trace(C) - 1.0)
    angle = np.arctan2(np.linalg.norm(w), cos_angle)     # better conditioned than arccos
    if angle < 1e-6:
        return (1.0 + angle**2 / 6.0) * w                # angle / sin(angle) ~ 1 + angle^2 / 6
    if np.pi - angle > 1e-4:
        return angle / np.sin(angle) * w
    # Near pi: (C + C^T)/2 = cos(angle) I + (1 - cos(angle)) u u^T gives the axis.
    uuT = (0.5 * (C + C.T) - cos_angle * np.eye(3)) / (1.0 - cos_angle)
    k = np.argmax(np.diag(uuT))
    u = uuT[:, k] / np.sqrt(uuT[k, k])
    return angle * (u if u @ w >= 0.0 else -u)          # sign from the skew part


def so3_right_jacobian(phi):
    """J_r(phi), with Exp(phi + d) ~= Exp(phi) Exp(J_r(phi) d)."""
    angle = np.linalg.norm(phi)
    K = skew(phi)
    if angle < 1e-6:
        return np.eye(3) - 0.5 * K + K @ K / 6.0
    return (np.eye(3) - (1.0 - np.cos(angle)) / angle**2 * K
            + (angle - np.sin(angle)) / angle**3 * K @ K)


def so3_left_jacobian(phi):
    """J_l(phi) = J_r(-phi), with Exp(phi + d) ~= Exp(J_l(phi) d) Exp(phi)."""
    return so3_right_jacobian(-phi)


def so3_right_jacobian_inv(phi):
    """Closed-form inverse of J_r(phi)."""
    angle = np.linalg.norm(phi)
    K = skew(phi)
    if angle < 1e-6:
        return np.eye(3) + 0.5 * K + K @ K / 12.0
    coef = 1.0 / angle**2 - (1.0 + np.cos(angle)) / (2.0 * angle * np.sin(angle))
    return np.eye(3) + 0.5 * K + coef * K @ K


def numerical_jacobian(f, x0, eps=1e-6):
    """Central-difference Jacobian of the vector function f at x0."""
    return np.column_stack([(f(x0 + d) - f(x0 - d)) / (2 * eps) for d in eps * np.eye(len(x0))])


rng = np.random.default_rng(11)

# 1. Exp agrees with SciPy, and Log inverts Exp, from tiny angles up to exactly pi.
worst = 0.0
for angle in [0.0, 1e-9, 1e-4, 0.3, 1.0, 2.5, np.pi - 1e-3, np.pi - 1e-6, np.pi]:
    for _ in range(50):
        axis = rng.normal(size=3)
        phi = angle * axis / np.linalg.norm(axis)
        C = so3_exp(phi)
        worst = max(worst, np.abs(C - Rotation.from_rotvec(phi).as_matrix()).max(),
                    np.abs(so3_exp(so3_log(C)) - C).max())
print(f"Exp vs SciPy and Exp(Log(C)) vs C, angles 0 to pi: worst error {worst:.1e}")

# 2. Jacobian definitions and identities at a decidedly non-small rotation.
phi = np.array([0.9, -1.4, 0.6])                         # |phi| = 1.77 rad, about 101 deg
C = so3_exp(phi)
zero = np.zeros(3)
checks = {
    "J_r vs Log(Exp(phi)^T Exp(phi + d))": np.abs(
        so3_right_jacobian(phi) - numerical_jacobian(lambda d: so3_log(C.T @ so3_exp(phi + d)), zero)),
    "J_l vs Log(Exp(phi + d) Exp(phi)^T)": np.abs(
        so3_left_jacobian(phi) - numerical_jacobian(lambda d: so3_log(so3_exp(phi + d) @ C.T), zero)),
    "J_r^-1 vs Log(C Exp(d))": np.abs(
        so3_right_jacobian_inv(phi) - numerical_jacobian(lambda d: so3_log(C @ so3_exp(d)), zero)),
    "J_l = Exp(phi) J_r": np.abs(so3_left_jacobian(phi) - C @ so3_right_jacobian(phi)),
    "adjoint: C Exp(v) C^T = Exp(C v)": np.abs(
        C @ so3_exp(np.array([0.1, 0.2, -0.3])) @ C.T - so3_exp(C @ np.array([0.1, 0.2, -0.3]))),
}
for name, err in checks.items():
    print(f"{name:38s} max error {err.max():.1e}")

# 3. The error-state reset (nav-frame error) is the left Jacobian.
dtheta_hat = np.deg2rad(3.0) * rng.standard_normal(3)    # an injected attitude correction
G = numerical_jacobian(lambda d: so3_log(so3_exp(d) @ so3_exp(-dtheta_hat)), dtheta_hat)
print(f"reset Jacobian: |G - J_l(dtheta_hat)| = {np.abs(G - so3_left_jacobian(dtheta_hat)).max():.1e},"
      f" |G - (I + [dtheta_hat/2]x)| = {np.abs(G - np.eye(3) - 0.5 * skew(dtheta_hat)).max():.1e}")
```

### Example: A Climbing Orbit With GNSS {#sec-advanced-slam-orbit-example}

Now a complete on-manifold problem that goes beyond the planar pose graph. An
inspection drone climbs in a spiral around a steel tower: 5 m/s on a 30 m
radius, climbing 0.4 m/s, banked into the turn, for 90 s. Visual-inertial
odometry provides a relative pose between consecutive 1 Hz keyframes, with 0.1 m
of noise per axis in translation and $0.5^\circ$ per axis in rotation. The
tower blocks much of the sky, so only one keyframe in six has a GNSS fix the
receiver trusts, with 1.5 m horizontal and 3 m vertical noise, measured at an
antenna 0.3 m forward of and 0.2 m above the IMU. And the drone took off next to
the steel tower, where its magnetometer was useless, so its initial heading
guess is $40^\circ$ wrong.

The variables are 90 poses on $SO(3) \times \mathbb{R}^3$, attitude
$\mathbf{C}_i = \mathbf{C}_{b_i}^n$ and position $\mathbf{p}_i$ in NED. The
factors are the relative-pose odometry of @eq-advanced-slam-relpose-factor and a
GNSS factor with a lever arm $\boldsymbol{\ell}^b$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{e}_k &= \mathbf{p}_k + \mathbf{C}_k\boldsymbol{\ell}^b - \tilde{\mathbf{z}}_k, \\
\frac{\partial\mathbf{e}_k}{\partial\delta\mathbf{x}_k} &=
\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{I} & -[\mathbf{C}_k\boldsymbol{\ell}^b]_\times \end{bmatrix},
\end{aligned}
$$

where the attitude column is the left-perturbation entry for
$\mathbf{C}\mathbf{v}$ in @tbl-advanced-slam-jacobians. There is no prior on the
first pose and no gauge to fix: with absolute position fixes spread around a
non-degenerate trajectory, every pose is determined, heading included. This is
the factor-graph version of the INS/GNSS heading alignment of @sec-ins-gnss, in
which heading becomes observable because the vehicle moves and turns.

::: {#advanced-slam-orbit-simulate .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)

# Truth: a coordinated, climbing right turn around a tower 30 m east of the start (NED).
n_kf, dt = 90, 1.0
speed, radius, climb, gravity = 5.0, 30.0, 0.4, 9.81
yaw_rate = speed / radius
bank = np.arctan(speed * yaw_rate / gravity)       # coordinated-turn roll, about 4.9 deg
pitch = np.arctan2(climb, speed)                    # flight-path angle, about 4.6 deg
C_true = np.array([Rotation.from_euler("ZYX", [yaw_rate * k * dt, pitch, bank]).as_matrix()
                   for k in range(n_kf)])
p_true = np.array([[radius * np.sin(yaw_rate * k * dt), radius * (1 - np.cos(yaw_rate * k * dt)),
                    -climb * k * dt] for k in range(n_kf)])

# VIO odometry: pose k+1 relative to body frame k, with noise.
sigma_odo = np.r_[np.full(3, 0.10), np.full(3, np.deg2rad(0.5))]    # [m]*3, [rad]*3
Omega_odo = np.diag(sigma_odo**-2.0)
odometry = []
for k in range(n_kf - 1):
    dC = C_true[k].T @ C_true[k + 1] @ so3_exp(rng.normal(0.0, sigma_odo[3:]))
    dp = C_true[k].T @ (p_true[k + 1] - p_true[k]) + rng.normal(0.0, sigma_odo[:3])
    odometry.append((k, k + 1, dC, dp))

# GNSS at one keyframe in six, antenna 0.3 m forward of and 0.2 m above the IMU (FRD).
lever_arm = np.array([0.3, 0.0, -0.2])
sigma_gnss = np.array([1.5, 1.5, 3.0])                              # N, E, D [m]
Omega_gnss = np.diag(sigma_gnss**-2.0)
gnss = [(k, p_true[k] + C_true[k] @ lever_arm + rng.normal(0.0, sigma_gnss))
        for k in range(0, n_kf, 6)]

# Initial guess: dead reckoning from the first fix, with the heading 40 deg wrong.
C_dr = [so3_exp(np.deg2rad([0.0, 0.0, 40.0])) @ C_true[0]]
p_dr = [gnss[0][1]]
for _, _, dC, dp in odometry:
    p_dr.append(p_dr[-1] + C_dr[-1] @ dp)
    C_dr.append(C_dr[-1] @ dC)
C_dr, p_dr = np.array(C_dr), np.array(p_dr)
print(f"{n_kf} keyframes, {len(odometry)} odometry factors, {len(gnss)} GNSS factors;"
      f" dead reckoning ends {np.linalg.norm(p_dr[-1] - p_true[-1]):.1f} m from the truth")
```

``` {.python .cell-code}
def odometry_factor(C_i, p_i, C_j, p_j, dC_meas, dp_meas):
    """Relative-pose residual [e_p; e_theta] and its Jacobians A = de/dx_i, B = de/dx_j.

    Perturbations are [dp; dtheta] with p <- p + dp and C <- Exp(dtheta) C
    (the book's navigation-frame attitude error).
    """
    d = p_j - p_i
    e_theta = so3_log(dC_meas.T @ C_i.T @ C_j)
    e = np.r_[C_i.T @ d - dp_meas, e_theta]
    Jr_inv = so3_right_jacobian_inv(e_theta)
    A, B = np.zeros((6, 6)), np.zeros((6, 6))
    A[:3, :3], A[:3, 3:] = -C_i.T, C_i.T @ skew(d)
    A[3:, 3:] = -Jr_inv @ C_j.T
    B[:3, :3] = C_i.T
    B[3:, 3:] = Jr_inv @ C_j.T
    return e, A, B


def gnss_factor(C_k, p_k, z):
    """Antenna position minus the fix, and its Jacobian with respect to [dp; dtheta]."""
    e = p_k + C_k @ lever_arm - z
    J = np.hstack([np.eye(3), -skew(C_k @ lever_arm)])
    return e, J


def oplus(C, p, dx):
    """Apply stacked corrections [dp_0, dtheta_0, dp_1, dtheta_1, ...] on the manifold."""
    dx = dx.reshape(-1, 6)
    return np.array([so3_exp(dth) @ Ck for Ck, dth in zip(C, dx[:, 3:])]), p + dx[:, :3]

    C2, p2 = C_dr.copy(), p_dr.copy()
```

## Marginalization and Fixed-Lag Smoothing {#sec-advanced-slam-marginalization}

### The Marginal Prior Factor {#sec-advanced-slam-marginal-prior}

A fixed-lag smoother keeps a window of recent states and must eventually let the
oldest ones go. Deleting them, together with their factors, would throw their
information away. **Marginalization** keeps the information and removes the
variables. Split the variables into those to marginalize, $\mathbf{x}_m$, and
those to keep, $\mathbf{x}_r$. Collect only the factors that touch
$\mathbf{x}_m$, linearize them at the current estimate $\bar{\mathbf{x}}$, and
write their contribution to the cost, $\tfrac{1}{2}\sum\mathbf{e}^T\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathbf{e}$,
as the quadratic $\tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\delta}^T\mathbf{H}\boldsymbol{\delta} + \mathbf{b}^T\boldsymbol{\delta}$
in the perturbation $\boldsymbol{\delta} = \mathbf{x} \ominus \bar{\mathbf{x}}$.
Minimizing over $\boldsymbol{\delta}_m$ leaves a quadratic in
$\boldsymbol{\delta}_r$ alone:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{H}^\star &= \mathbf{H}_{rr} - \mathbf{H}_{rm}\mathbf{H}_{mm}^{-1}\mathbf{H}_{mr}, \\
\mathbf{b}^\star &= \mathbf{b}_r - \mathbf{H}_{rm}\mathbf{H}_{mm}^{-1}\mathbf{b}_m, \\
c(\boldsymbol{\delta}_r) &= \tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\delta}_r^T\mathbf{H}^\star\boldsymbol{\delta}_r + \mathbf{b}^{\star T}\boldsymbol{\delta}_r + \text{const}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-advanced-slam-marginal-prior}

This is the Schur complement of @eq-information-marginal applied to the
linearized problem, and it is the same algebra as the reduced camera system of
@eq-visual-nav-schur. The difference is intent. Bundle adjustment eliminates
the points temporarily, to solve faster, and recovers them by back-substitution.
Marginalization eliminates $\mathbf{x}_m$ permanently. The quadratic
$c(\boldsymbol{\delta}_r)$ becomes a new **marginal prior factor** on the kept
variables; factoring $\mathbf{H}^\star = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^T$ puts it in the
same form as every other factor, with residual
$\mathbf{e}_\text{prior} = \mathbf{L}^T(\mathbf{x}_r \ominus \bar{\mathbf{x}}_r) + \mathbf{L}^{-1}\mathbf{b}^\star$
and unit information.

The marginal prior connects every variable that shared a factor with
$\mathbf{x}_m$ (its *Markov blanket*), so it is generally a dense factor over
all of them. Marginalize an old keyframe in a visual-inertial window and the
prior links the next keyframe's pose, velocity, and biases with every landmark
the old keyframe saw. Do that repeatedly and the window's information matrix
fills in, the slow-motion version of @fig-information-fill-in. Sliding-window
VIO systems therefore marginalize carefully. OKVIS [@leutenegger2015okvis] and
VINS-Mono [@qin2018vins] marginalize the oldest keyframe together with the
landmarks anchored in it, but when a recent frame turns out not to be a keyframe
they *drop* its visual measurements rather than marginalize them, keeping only
the IMU chain through it. Dropping throws information away, which is
conservative; marginalizing keeps it, at the price of density. The MSCKF's
null-space projection (@sec-visual-nav-msckf) is marginalization in disguise: on
the linearized problem, the projected residuals carry exactly the information
about the states that the Schur complement of the feature would leave.

### First-Estimates Jacobians and Consistency {#sec-advanced-slam-fej}

Marginalization has a subtler cost in nonlinear problems. The prior factor is a
*linearization*, frozen at $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_r$ forever. The variables it
constrains stay in the window and keep moving, and the new factors attached to
them are linearized at their newer estimates. The information matrix then mixes
Jacobians evaluated at different points for the same variable, and that can
manufacture information that no measurement contains.

The damage happens along the unobservable directions. In planar SLAM with
relative measurements, translating or rotating the whole problem changes no
residual, so the information matrix has a three-dimensional null space (Exercise
2 of the loop-closure chapter finds it). The translation directions are the same
at every estimate, but the rotation direction is not: rotating the world about
the origin moves pose $i$ along $[-y_i,\ x_i,\ 1]^T$, which depends on where the
estimate puts the pose. A prior linearized at $\bar{\mathbf{x}}$ has the
rotation null vector of $\bar{\mathbf{x}}$; a new factor linearized at
$\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ has that of $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$. Their sum has no common null
vector for rotation, so the estimator acquires information about the global
heading, from measurements that contain none. Huang, Mourikis, and Roumeliotis
traced EKF-SLAM inconsistency to exactly this mechanism [@huang2010], and it is
the reason VIO filters become overconfident in yaw
(@sec-visual-nav-vio-observability).

The fix is almost embarrassingly simple. **First-estimates Jacobians** (FEJ)
evaluate the Jacobians of every factor that involves a variable in the marginal
prior at that variable's first estimate, the point where the prior was
linearized, while the residuals still use the current estimate
[@huang2010]. Every Jacobian of a given variable then shares one linearization
point, and the null space survives. The price is slightly less accurate
Jacobians, which is small while estimates stay close to their first values.
Observability-constrained filters project the Jacobians onto the correct null
space instead [@hesch2014consistency], and the invariant EKF chooses an error
definition on the group for which the troublesome Jacobians do not depend on the
estimate at all [@barrau2017iekf]. OpenVINS uses FEJ throughout, and every
sliding-window optimizer must at least hold its marginal prior at the prior's own
linearization point, since a frozen quadratic cannot be relinearized.

The cell below makes the mechanism visible on the smallest example that shows
it: planar poses $x_0, x_1, x_2$ and landmarks $l_0, l_1$, with odometry and
landmark observations in the robot frame. Pose $x_0$ is marginalized at the
first estimates; the new factors (odometry $x_1 \to x_2$ and $x_2$ observing both
landmarks) are then linearized either at the current estimates (standard) or
with FEJ. With no absolute measurement anywhere, the information matrix should
have three zero eigenvalues. To turn "spurious information" into a number, the
cell also anchors the position of $x_1$, as a single GNSS fix would, and asks
how well the estimator then claims to know the heading.

``` {.python .cell-code}
def rot2(theta):
    c, s = np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)
    return np.array([[c, -s], [s, c]])


def drot2T(theta):
    """Derivative of rot2(theta)^T with respect to theta."""
    c, s = np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)
    return np.array([[-s, c], [-c, -s]])


def odometry_jacobians(xa, xb):
    """Jacobians of e = [C_a^T (t_b - t_a) - z_t; theta_b - theta_a - z_theta]."""
    A, B = np.zeros((3, 3)), np.zeros((3, 3))
    A[:2, :2], A[:2, 2], A[2, 2] = -rot2(xa[2]).T, drot2T(xa[2]) @ (xb[:2] - xa[:2]), -1.0
    B[:2, :2], B[2, 2] = rot2(xa[2]).T, 1.0
    return A, B, np.diag(1.0 / np.array([0.1, 0.1, 0.02]) ** 2)


def observation_jacobians(x, landmark):
    """Jacobians of e = C^T (l - t) - z: a landmark position in the robot frame."""
    A = np.hstack([-rot2(x[2]).T, (drot2T(x[2]) @ (landmark - x[:2]))[:, None]])
    return A, rot2(x[2]).T, np.eye(2) / 0.1**2


layout = {"x0": slice(0, 3), "x1": slice(3, 6), "x2": slice(6, 9), "l0": slice(9, 11), "l1": slice(11, 13)}
n_fej = 13


def information(factor_list, estimate):
    """Gauss-Newton information matrix of the listed factors, linearized at `estimate`."""
    H_f = np.zeros((n_fej, n_fej))
    for kind, a, c in factor_list:
        jac = odometry_jacobians if kind == "odometry" else observation_jacobians
        A, B, W = jac(estimate[a], estimate[c])
        J = np.zeros((A.shape[0], n_fej))
        J[:, layout[a]], J[:, layout[c]] = A, B
        H_f += J.T @ W @ J
    return H_f


old_factors = [("odometry", "x0", "x1"), ("observation", "x0", "l0"), ("observation", "x0", "l1"),
               ("observation", "x1", "l0"), ("observation", "x1", "l1")]
new_factors = [("odometry", "x1", "x2"), ("observation", "x2", "l0"), ("observation", "x2", "l1")]
truth_fej = {"x0": np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.1]), "x1": np.array([1.0, 0.2, 0.3]),
             "x2": np.array([2.0, 0.6, 0.5]), "l0": np.array([1.5, 2.0]), "l1": np.array([2.5, -1.0])}
first = {v: x + rng.normal(0, 0.05, x.shape) for v, x in truth_fej.items()}    # first estimates
step = {v: (np.r_[rng.normal(0, 0.1, 2), rng.normal(0, np.deg2rad(2))] if len(x) == 3
            else rng.normal(0, 0.1, 2)) for v, x in truth_fej.items()}            # later updates

# Marginalize x0 out of the old factors, linearized at the first estimates.
H_old = information(old_factors, first)
keep, drop = np.arange(3, n_fej), np.arange(0, 3)
prior = H_old[np.ix_(keep, keep)] - H_old[np.ix_(keep, drop)] @ np.linalg.solve(
    H_old[np.ix_(drop, drop)], H_old[np.ix_(drop, keep)])


def heading_sigma_deg(H_k):
    """Anchor x1's position (delete its rows) and return the claimed 1-sigma heading of x1."""
    sub = np.arange(2, H_k.shape[0])
    H_sub = H_k[np.ix_(sub, sub)]
    eig = np.linalg.eigvalsh(H_sub)
    return np.inf if eig[0] < 1e-9 * eig[-1] else np.degrees(np.sqrt(np.linalg.inv(H_sub)[0, 0]))


for scale in [0.0, 1.0, 3.0, 10.0]:
    current = {v: first[v] + scale * step[v] for v in first}
    fej = dict(current, x1=first["x1"], l0=first["l0"], l1=first["l1"])        # old variables at first estimates
    results = []
    for estimate in (current, fej):
        H_total = prior + information(new_factors, estimate)[np.ix_(keep, keep)]
        results.append((np.linalg.eigvalsh(H_total)[:3], heading_sigma_deg(H_total)))
    (eig_std, sig_std), (eig_fej, sig_fej) = results
    print(f"update x{scale:<4}: standard eigenvalues {np.array2string(eig_std, precision=1)},"
          f" heading sigma {sig_std:6.1f} deg | FEJ heading sigma {sig_fej:.1f} deg")
```

With no update between marginalization and the new factors (scale 0), both
versions agree: three zero eigenvalues, and an infinite heading uncertainty,
which is the truth, since nothing in this problem measures heading. As soon as
the estimates move, the standard version's third eigenvalue lifts off zero and
the estimator claims a finite heading uncertainty: about $120^\circ$ after an
update of typical size (0.1 m and $2^\circ$ per variable), $40^\circ$ after one
three times larger, and $12^\circ$ after one ten times larger. A
$120^\circ$ sigma sounds harmless, but the honest answer is "no idea," and the
claimed information grows with the square of the update. FEJ keeps all three
null directions at every update size. One marginalization step manufactures
only a little information, but a sliding window marginalizes at every keyframe
and the spurious information accumulates, so over a long run the claimed yaw
uncertainty keeps shrinking while the true yaw error keeps drifting
(Exercise 4). That is what inconsistency looks like in the field: not a crash,
but a confident estimator that is wrong.

## GNSS-Denied and Resilient Navigation {#sec-advanced-slam-gnss-denied-resilient}

GNSS-denied navigation means operating when satellite positioning is
unavailable, degraded, or attacked: indoors, underground, underwater, in urban
canyons, under foliage, near large steel structures, and increasingly anywhere
near jamming and spoofing. The receiver-level side of the problem (signals,
tight and deep coupling, integrity, interference) is the subject of
@sec-adv-gnss; this section is about what replaces or backs up GNSS.

No single aid solves the problem, so resilient systems layer them, each with a
different failure mode (@tbl-advanced-slam-resilient):

| Aid | Useful when | Main weakness |
|---|---|---|
| Visual or lidar odometry | texture or geometric structure is visible | darkness, blur, dust, featureless corridors |
| Radar odometry | weather, dust, smoke, long range | low angular resolution, hard data association |
| Terrain or bathymetric navigation | a good elevation or depth map exists | flat or repetitive terrain |
| Magnetic anomaly navigation | a crustal anomaly map exists | vehicle's own magnetic field, map resolution |
| Celestial navigation | stars are visible (even by day, with the right sensor) | weather, attitude accuracy needed |
| Signals of opportunity, LEO PNT | radio infrastructure or satellites in view | opportunistic geometry, unknown clocks |
| Barometer, depth, wheel or DVL odometry | always, for one axis or for velocity | weather, slip, currents, calibration |
| Cooperative localization | other agents are nearby | communication, shared-frame uncertainty |

: Layers of resilient navigation. {#tbl-advanced-slam-resilient}

Map-matching aids are the oldest. Terrain-aided navigation compares radar
altimeter clearance with a stored elevation map and has guided cruise missiles
since the 1970s; @sec-pf-terrain-aided-navigation builds one with a particle
filter [@gustafsson2002]. **Magnetic anomaly navigation** does the same with the
crustal magnetic field, whose anomalies vary over hundreds of meters to tens of
kilometers and have been mapped by geological surveys. It is passive and
unjammable, and flight tests have shown useful accuracy [@canciani2017magnav];
its hard part is not the filter but removing the aircraft's own magnetic
signature, a calibration problem attacked with the Tolles-Lawson model, first
developed around 1950 for submarine-hunting aircraft. Celestial navigation, the
oldest of all [@bowditch2019], has returned as star trackers small enough for
aircraft and ships; the SR-71's astro-inertial system tracked stars in daylight
half a century ago.

Radio alternatives are growing quickly. **Signals of opportunity** (cellular,
broadcast, and the downlinks of low-Earth-orbit communication constellations)
were never designed for navigation, so the receiver must estimate the
transmitters' clocks and sometimes their positions along with its own state.
**LEO PNT** services are designed for it: an Iridium-based timing and location
service is operational, and several dedicated LEO navigation constellations are
in development, attractive because LEO signals arrive far stronger than GNSS
signals from 20,000 km and sweep across the sky quickly, which helps geometry.
Terrestrial low-frequency systems such as eLoran are being deployed or
proposed as national backups in several countries.

In factor-graph terms every one of these is just another factor, which is the
practical argument for graph back ends in resilient navigation: adding an aid
means adding a residual and a noise model. Integrity generalizes the same way.
RAIM (@sec-adv-gnss-raim) tests whether the least-squares residuals are larger
than chance allows; a smoother can run the same chi-square test on its total
cost, as the orbit example did, and the normalized residuals point at the factor
that is lying. The professional habit is graceful degradation: when an aid drops
out, change mode, grow the uncertainty honestly, report it downstream, and log
enough to explain the outage afterward.

## Advanced SLAM and Mapping {#sec-advanced-slam-mapping}

The SLAM module covered EKF-SLAM, FastSLAM, GraphSLAM, visual SLAM, and loop
closure. Modern systems push those ideas along several axes at once.

**Lidar-inertial odometry** is the workhorse of ground and aerial robots that can
afford a lidar, and its two best-known open systems neatly illustrate the
filter-smoother split of @tbl-advanced-slam-spectrum. LIO-SAM [@shan2020liosam]
is a factor graph solved with iSAM2: preintegrated IMU factors, lidar odometry
factors from scan-to-local-map matching on keyframes, optional GNSS factors, and
loop-closure factors, exactly the ingredients of @fig-advanced-slam-factor-graph
with a lidar in place of the camera. FAST-LIO2 [@xu2022fastlio2] is a tightly
coupled iterated error-state Kalman filter that registers raw points directly to
the map, with no feature extraction, and keeps the map in an incremental k-d tree;
it runs comfortably on small onboard computers. Both are excellent, which says
something about the filter-versus-smoother debate.

**Dense, semantic, and neural maps** describe more than sparse landmarks. Dense
maps reconstruct surfaces, occupancy, or signed distance fields; semantic maps
attach labels such as road, building, vehicle, buoy, or runway; dynamic maps try
to separate persistent structure from moving objects. Neural radiance fields and
3D Gaussian splatting represent scenes with learned functions or millions of
small Gaussians and produce striking reconstructions. For navigation they raise
hard questions about real-time cost, uncertainty, and validation, but they are
moving into SLAM quickly (@sec-advanced-slam-learning-based-emerging).

**Multi-robot and lifelong SLAM** ask what happens when several agents share a
map, or one agent revisits a changing environment for months. Inter-robot loop
closures are the most valuable and the most dangerous measurements in such a
system, so consistency checks such as PCM (@sec-loop-closure-robust-kernels)
were developed for exactly this setting. Distributed solvers optimize a shared
pose graph without sending all data to one place. Lifelong mapping must bound
map growth, retire stale observations, and cope with robots whose sensors,
clocks, and frames differ. These problems matter for fleets in warehouses,
ports, mines, farms, and survey operations, and they are as much about
communication and data management as about estimation.

## Rao-Blackwellized and Hybrid Filters {#sec-advanced-slam-rao-blackwellized-hybrid}

FastSLAM is a Rao-Blackwellized particle filter (@sec-slam,
@sec-pf-rao-blackwellized): sample the hard part of the state (the robot's path)
and solve the conditionally easy part (each landmark, given the path) in closed
form. In the vocabulary of this chapter, Rao-Blackwellization is marginalization
done analytically inside each sample, and it is the same structural insight that
makes factor graphs sparse: conditional independence turns one large problem
into many small ones.

The pattern recurs wherever a navigation posterior is part discrete, part
continuous, or multimodal: sampling or enumerating discrete mode hypotheses
(which aid is faulty, which data association is right, which map tile the
vehicle is on) while filtering the continuous state; marginalized particle
filters for terrain navigation, with a small Kalman filter per particle for the
linear velocity and bias states [@gustafsson2002]; and, on the smoothing side,
multi-hypothesis factors such as the switchable constraints of
@sec-loop-closure-robust-kernels. Hybrid methods are attractive when one
Gaussian is too few and a full particle filter too many. They are also easy to
misuse: particle depletion, poor proposals, overconfident likelihoods, and
missing resampling diagnostics can make a hybrid filter look sophisticated while
it quietly discards the correct hypothesis.

## Learning-Based and Emerging Methods {#sec-advanced-slam-learning-based-emerging}

Machine learning has entered navigation mostly by replacing *components*, not
the estimator. The learned front ends of @sec-visual-nav-learned-front-ends are
one example: networks produce keypoints and matches, and geometry turns them into
motion. Three newer directions are worth knowing.

**Learned inertial odometry** regresses motion directly from IMU data. TLIO
[@liu2020tlio] trains a network on pedestrian motion to predict displacement over
a short window of gravity-aligned IMU samples, together with a covariance for
that displacement, and fuses the prediction as a measurement in an error-state
EKF that also estimates the IMU biases. The network supplies a motion prior that
pure integration lacks (people walk in recognizable ways) and the filter supplies
consistency and bias estimation. **Learned dense SLAM** puts a network inside the
optimization: DROID-SLAM [@teed2021droid] refines dense optical flow with a
recurrent network and turns it into poses and depths with a differentiable
bundle-adjustment layer. MASt3R-SLAM [@murai2025mast3rslam] builds real-time
dense monocular SLAM on a pretrained two-view 3D reconstruction network, a
"foundation model" for geometry, and assumes little about the camera beyond a
single center of projection. **Other emerging sensing** includes event cameras,
which report per-pixel brightness changes with microsecond timing and no motion
blur, and radar-inertial odometry for weather and smoke that blind cameras and
lidars.

The hard part is evaluating learned components honestly, and the questions are
the ones this book has asked of every estimator. **Generalization**: was the
method tested on environments, platforms, and sensors that were not in the
training set, or on held-out minutes of the same recordings? A network trained
on pedestrians knows nothing about a quadrotor, and one trained in summer may
not recognize the same street in snow. **Uncertainty calibration**: a learned
covariance is a measurement noise model and must pass the same NIS and NEES
tests as any other (@sec-kf-nees-nis). Networks are routinely overconfident
exactly where the data were sparse, so check calibration by operating regime
(turning versus straight, fast versus slow), not just on average.
**Consistency inside the estimator**: overlapping input windows produce
correlated errors, which violates the white-noise assumption of the filter
fusing them; ignoring that is overconfidence by construction. **Failure
detection**: does the system know when an input is unlike anything it was
trained on? **Cost**: a method that needs a desktop GPU is not a drop-in for a
250 g drone. A learned component that passes these tests is a powerful sensor.
One that has only been tested on its benchmark is a hypothesis.

## How to Read the Research Literature {#sec-advanced-slam-how-read-research}

Navigation papers are hard to compare because they differ in sensors, datasets,
compute, initialization, and in what they count as success. A few questions
cut through most of it. What sensors are actually used, and how were they
calibrated and synchronized? Is the method a filter, a smoother, learned, or a
hybrid, and does it run online, in real time on stated hardware, or offline? What
bounds global drift: GNSS, loop closure, a prior map, or nothing (in which case
the honest metric is drift per distance traveled)? How are outliers and dropouts
handled, and are failures reported or are only the successful sequences shown?
Are uncertainty estimates checked for consistency, or merely plotted?

Read the evaluation protocol as carefully as the method. Absolute trajectory
error is computed after aligning the estimate to ground truth, and the alignment
matters: $SE(3)$ for stereo visual odometry, four degrees of freedom (position
and yaw) for VIO, because those are exactly its unobservable directions, and
$\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ for monocular systems, which forgives scale errors that may be
the method's main weakness [@zhang2018trajectory]. Relative pose error over
fixed distances measures drift and is harder to game. Results averaged over several runs, with the failure rate
reported, are worth more than a single best run. And treat "real time,"
"robust," and "state of the art" as claims relative to a platform, a dataset, a
sensor suite, and an operating environment, never as properties of an algorithm.

## Summary {#sec-advanced-slam-summary}

1. A factor graph turns navigation into sparse nonlinear least squares: variables
   for the unknowns, factors for measurements, motion models, and priors. The
   sparsity of the information matrix is the graph.
2. Filtering, fixed-lag smoothing, and full smoothing differ in which variables
   they keep and what they relinearize. On a linear chain the Kalman filter is
   the forward elimination sweep and the RTS smoother the back-substitution.
3. Eliminating a variable is marginalizing it and connects its neighbors.
   Variable ordering controls the fill-in; incremental solvers such as iSAM2
   reuse everything a new factor does not touch.
4. Attitudes and poses live on Lie groups. Exp, Log, $\oplus$, $\ominus$, the
   left and right Jacobians, and the adjoint make Gauss-Newton and covariance
   work on them. The book's attitude error is a left (navigation-frame)
   perturbation, and the error-state filter is a one-step on-manifold
   Gauss-Newton with a reset Jacobian equal to $\mathbf{J}_l$.
5. Marginalization in a sliding window produces a dense prior factor on the
   Markov blanket. Its frozen linearization point can manufacture information
   along unobservable directions; first-estimates Jacobians prevent that.
6. Resilient navigation, lidar-inertial and dense mapping, hybrid filters, and
   learned components all fit into the same framework, and all must be judged by
   the same standards of consistency and honest evaluation.
